newsitem.title: ITALY: Chronology of Priebke and Hass war crimes trials.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Priebke and Hass war crimes trials.

text.p: The war crimes trials of former SS officers Erich Priebke and Karl Hass for Italy's worst World War Two massacre have been an emotional roller-coaster ride of painful memories, high drama and judicial hair-splitting.

Following are key events in the two trials, the second of which ended on Tuesday when Priebke, a former Nazi SS captain, was sentenced to five years in jail and Hass, who held the rank of major, was set free.
Nov 21, 1995 - Priebke is extradited to Italy from Argentina, where he had lived openly since 1948. Under intense security, he is taken to a military jail in Rome.
Dec 7 - Priebke is brought to court for the first time. Relations of victims of the SS massacre of 335 men and boys at the Ardeatine Caves in 1944 shout "assassin" as he is led in.
April 4, 1996 - An examining judge orders Priebke to trial from May 8, 51st anniversary of end of World War Two in Europe.
May 8 - Priebke's trial opens in cramped courtroom. Judges refuse to move to larger premises.

June 3 - Prosecution calls Priebke to witness stand. He refuses to answer questions about the massacre and submits a written statement saying officers were told they had to take part or be killed themselves.
June 7 - Karl Hass, an 84-year-old former SS major and key prosecution witness falls from first-floor balcony of his hotel room and fractures his pelvis trying to avoid testifying.
June 12 - Trial moves to hospital where Hass gives evidence from his bed.

June 27 - Case takes a soap-opera twist when Priebke's lawyer denies allegations that Priebke bribed a court official. He says the accuser, Italian writer Mary Pace, who had befriended the defendant, was seeking revenge after Priebke rejected her romantic advances.
June 28 - Trial thrown into chaos when prosecution asks the three-judge bench to step down because of "irregularities" in the way the case was being handled. Trial suspended.
July 11 - Trial reopens. Prosecution asks court to impose a life sentence.
July 29 - Priebke turns 83. Attends appeals court hearing.
July 30 - Defence calls for Priebke's acquittal.

Aug 1 - Court issues verdict, ruling that while Priebke was responsible for killings, extenuating circumstances and a statute of limitations meant he would go unpunished. Uproar breaks out and protesters lay siege to coutroom. Priebke is re-arrested after several hours. Verdict condemned in Italy.
Oct 15 - Italy's highest court of appeal, the Court of Cassation, overturns the August verdict and orders a retrial.
Nov 26 - Arrest warrant issued for Hass, who is seized and placed under house arrest.
Dec 5 - Military tribunal in Rome rules the cases of both Priebke and Hass are outside their jurisdiction. Case handed over to public prosecutors.
Dec 14 - Rome public prosecutors likewise say they have no jurisdiction over the case, triggering arguments over which branch of the judiciary should oversee the re-trial.
Feb 10 1997 - Court of Cassation ends dispute, ruling that Priebke and Hass should be tried together, by military court.
March 3 - Italy's Constitutional court rules that Priebke cannot be extradited to Germany, as had been requested, as he already faces war crimes charges in Italy.
March 18 - Military court orders both Priebke and Hass to be placed under house arrest.
March 21 - Priebke taken to Roman Catholic convent Rome where he is held pending the re-trial.
April 14 - Re-trial of Priebke and trial of Hass begins in courtroom in Rome's high-security Rebibbia prison.
June 27 - Prosecution lawyers call for life sentence for Priebke and 24-year sentence for Hass.
July 1 - Lawyer for the city of Rome calls for five life sentences for both Priebke and Hass.
July 14 - Defence pleads for clemency, saying Priebke and Hass were simply obeying orders.
July 22 - Three-judge panel convicts both Priebke and Hass and sentences Priebke to 15 years and Hass to 10 years and eight months because of mitigating circumstances.

Judges reduce the terms by a further 10 years in each case because of other concessions. Hass is allowed to go free because he has already been held under house arrest. Priebke, who has been detained for some 3-1/2 years in Argentina and Italy, now faces around 1-1/2 years in jail.
